sections.h2: Which Johnson County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
Three desks share the work in Johnson County: the Property Valuation Administrator (PVA) sets values, the sheriff collects, and the county clerk records liens and takes appeals. Knowing which one to call saves a lot of transfers.

County offices cluster at 230 Court Street in Paintsville. The clerk is in Suite 124 at (606) 789-2557 and keeps weekday hours from 8 to 4, with no Saturday service. The sheriff's page lists (606) 789-3411 and the same weekday hours.

The PVA does not set rates. The Fiscal Court meets the second Monday of each month at 4:45 PM, and the county's two public school systems, Johnson County Schools and Paintsville Independent, are among the bodies that levy tax on a bill.

sections.h2: What is the yearly property tax calendar in Johnson County?
sections.html:
The assessment half of the year is fixed by state law and works the same in Johnson County as anywhere in Kentucky. For homeowners the key date is the first Monday in May, when a 13-day inspection window begins.

Kentucky tax calendar milestones that govern a Johnson County parcel
MilestoneWhen
Value is fixed as ofJanuary 1
Owners list real estateJanuary 1 through March 1
Tax roll open, PVA conferences held13 days from the first Monday in May, including Saturdays
Appeal filed at the clerkBy the end of the next workday after inspection
Local board hearingsUp to five days, opening 25 to 35 days after inspection
Business and other personal propertyListed January 1 through May 15

Source: Kentucky Department of Revenue, The Property Tax Calendar.

Bills follow in the fall. Kentucky's usual pattern gives 2 percent off through November 1, face value to year end, a 5 percent penalty in January and heavier charges after that. Ask the Johnson County Sheriff for this year's exact dates.

sections.h2: What happens to an unpaid Johnson County bill?
sections.html:
On April 15 the sheriff hands any unpaid bill to the Johnson County Clerk. The clerk records a lien, and the bill can end up in the hands of a private buyer.

State revenue officials lay out the sequence: 1 percent monthly interest starts at transfer, the county attorney sends notices, the clerk advertises the list 30 to 45 days ahead of a sale, and the sale itself falls 90 to 135 days after transfer under KRS 134.128. Counties that also sell delinquent oil and gas or unmined mineral bills get 60 extra days, a rule that fits a coalfield county where such interests are billed separately.

  • The lien attaches to the land, so it passes to a new owner unless paid.
  • A purchaser of the bill can charge its own fees on top.
  • Notices travel by regular mail to the address on file.

sections.h2: What is the appeal route for a Johnson County value?
sections.html:
Go to the PVA office during the May window and ask for a conference. Kentucky bars a filing with the board until that talk has taken place, and the PVA has to walk you through how the figure was reached.

If the talk fails, file with the county clerk by the close of the next workday after inspection ends. A board of local property owners hears the case with the clerk's office acting as its clerk. The board must deny an appeal that arrives without facts to support it, such as insurance policies, building costs, listings or a description of the land and structures.

  • Request the list of sales the PVA used for your house.
  • Collect repair quotes if damage is not on the record.
  • Hired representatives must fit state categories, including attorneys, CPAs and licensed appraisers.

The final stop is the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals. With median values near $120,000, a change of a few thousand dollars in value still moves a bill, so one phone call is cheap.

sections.h2: Who can claim a homestead or other exemption in Johnson County?
sections.html:
Owners 65 and over, and owners totally disabled under a federal or retirement program, can take the homestead and disability deduction. Only one exemption fits a household, and it follows the owner, so a buyer files a new application.

The deduction is a set dollar amount that Kentucky revises every two years. Another county's PVA lists $49,100 for 2025 to 2026, so check with the Johnson PVA for the figure on your bill. Totally disabled veterans, and people found disabled under Social Security or Kentucky Retirement rules, file once. Owners classed disabled by an out-of-state agency must refile annually.

Churches, schools and charities use Revenue Form 62A023. Farmland is valued by use, which the state says can cut a bill sharply where market and farm values diverge. Separately from property tax, the county charges an occupational tax of 0.5 percent on wages and net profit earned inside Johnson County.

sections.h2: What does Johnson County's housing profile look like?
sections.html:
Homes here cost far less than the Kentucky metro norm. The 2020 to 2024 Census survey gives a $120,200 median value, a $44,904 median household income and a $708 median gross rent, with 20.9 percent of residents in poverty.

The county has 10,714 housing units, and 68.3 percent of occupied homes are lived in by owners. Population was 22,680 in 2020 and an estimated 22,051 in July 2025, a drop of 2.8 percent. Its peak came in 1940 at 25,771, and 12.0 percent of housing units were vacant in 2020, against 5.8 percent in Jessamine County and 6.9 percent in Kenton County.

Floodplain rules touch some parcels. Building in a Special Flood Hazard Area needs both a state and a local permit, and the county asks owners to call (606) 789-2550 before any development.

sections.h2: How did Johnson County's coal and oil history shape its parcels?
sections.html:
The railroad reached Paintsville in 1904 and opened the coal era, which lasted more than a century. Consolidation Coal and North East Coal built the towns of Van Lear and Thealka, and by the 1940s as many as 1,500 men worked the county's mines.

Oil and gas followed from 1917, and in 1922 the Johnson-Magoffin field produced over 2,000,000 barrels. Coal output peaked in 2008 at 2,713,196 tons. Wikipedia adds that many residents sold their mineral rights cheaply during the coal boom.

For a seller, that history is practical. Ask your title company whether minerals were severed from the surface on your parcel, and ask the sheriff whether any separately billed mineral or oil and gas tax bill is tied to it.

sections.h2: What should a Johnson County seller confirm before closing?
sections.html:
Make three calls: the sheriff for the current bill and payoff, the clerk for any certificate of delinquency, and the PVA for the exemption status. Together they cover nearly every tax surprise.

The county lists separate fire and rescue units for Paintsville, Van Lear, West Van Lear and others, and a Kentucky bill can stack school, city, county and fire levies. Ask the sheriff for a line-by-line breakdown. The Kenton County Sheriff notes that sellers settle their share of the year with the buyer at closing and the owner of record pays the whole bill.

faqs.q: Which office collects Johnson County property tax?
faqs.a: The Johnson County Sheriff. The office lists (606) 789-3411 and keeps weekday hours from 8 to 4.

faqs.q: Where is a Johnson County assessment appeal filed?
faqs.a: At the county clerk's office, 230 Court Street, Suite 124, Paintsville, after a PVA conference. The deadline is the end of the workday after the May inspection window closes.

faqs.q: When does an unpaid Johnson County bill move to the clerk?
faqs.a: At the close of business on April 15. The clerk then holds it as a certificate of delinquency with a recorded lien.

faqs.q: Does a Johnson County homeowner get the 65 exemption automatically?
faqs.a: No. You apply through the PVA, you must live in the home, and the state allows one exemption per household.

faqs.q: Who decides Johnson County tax rates?
faqs.a: The taxing bodies on your bill, such as the Fiscal Court and the school districts. The PVA values property and the sheriff collects.
